title: Jeremiah 24:1–10
context: Jeremiah reports a vision the LORD showed him after Nebuchadnezzar carried Jeconiah, the princes, and the craftsmen and smiths to Babylon, an exile commonly dated to 597 BC and narrated in 2 Kings 24:10–17. The good figs are the exiles, whom the LORD will bring back, build, and plant, giving them “a heart to know me” (24:5–7); the bad figs are Zedekiah, his princes, the remnant in Jerusalem, and those in Egypt, who face judgment (24:8–10). Jeremiah 29:17 reuses the bad-figs image. On the promised heart, see the existing Deuteronomy 10:16 and 5:29 boxes.

verses.text: The LORD showed me, and behold, two baskets of figs were set before the LORD’s temple, after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and the princes of Judah, with the craftsmen and smiths, from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah reports, “The LORD showed me,” two baskets of figs before the temple after Nebuchadnezzar carried away Jeconiah. Arminian readers see a vision interpreting the first deportation, narrated in 2 Kings 24.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the vision set after Jeconiah’s exile, commonly dated to 597 BC, with 2 Kings 24:10–17 cited by reference. Readers in this tradition note that the vision interprets events the people found hard to understand.

verses.text: One basket had very good figs, like the figs that are first-ripe; and the other basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad.
verses.arminianNotes: “One basket had very good figs, like the figs that are first-ripe; and the other basket had very bad figs.” Arminian readers see a simple contrast that the LORD will interpret for the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a stark visual contrast. Readers in this tradition note that the meaning is not obvious until God explains it, which keeps the interpretation in his hands rather than the prophet’s.

verses.text: Then the LORD asked me, “What do you see, Jeremiah?” I said, “Figs. The good figs are very good, and the bad are very bad, so bad that they can’t be eaten.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “What do you see, Jeremiah?” and he answers, “Figs.” Arminian readers see the LORD drawing the prophet into the vision, as in Jeremiah 1:11–13, cited by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the familiar pattern of question and answer in prophetic visions. Readers in this tradition note that Jeremiah describes what he sees, and the LORD supplies the meaning.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s word came to me, saying,” introduces the interpretation. Arminian readers see the vision explained by God’s word rather than left to speculation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the vision subordinated to the word that follows. Readers in this tradition stress that visions in Scripture are interpreted by God’s word, which matches the concern of chapter 23 about dreams.

verses.text: “The LORD, the God of Israel says: ‘Like these good figs, so I will regard the captives of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans, as good.
verses.arminianNotes: “Like these good figs, so I will regard the captives of Judah … as good.” Arminian readers see a surprising reversal: the exiles, not those left behind, are the object of God’s favor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal of expectations. Those who stayed in Jerusalem may have thought themselves favored, but the LORD declares his gracious purpose toward the exiles.

verses.text: For I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them again to this land. I will build them, and not pull them down. I will plant them, and not pluck them up.
verses.arminianNotes: “For I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them again to this land.” Arminian readers see God’s promise to build and plant, echoing the language of Jeremiah 1:10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant mercy in the promise to build and plant. Readers in this tradition note the echo of the prophet’s commission in 1:10 and see the LORD fulfilling his word of restoration.

verses.text: I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD. They will be my people, and I will be their God; for they will return to me with their whole heart.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will give them a heart to know me.” Arminian readers hear God’s gracious enabling, received as the people return; the Deuteronomy 10:16 and 5:29 boxes set out how this tradition relates grace and response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear God giving the heart that makes return certain, so that “they will return to me with their whole heart” follows the gift. The existing Deuteronomy 10:16 and 5:29 boxes cover this difference.

verses.text: “ ‘As the bad figs, which can’t be eaten, they are so bad,’ surely the LORD says, ‘So I will give up Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: “As the bad figs … So I will give up Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the remnant of Jerusalem.” Arminian readers see judgment on those who remained and trusted in their position.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment on Zedekiah and those left behind, including those in Egypt. The text does not explain why some were in Egypt, and readers in this tradition avoid speculating beyond it.

verses.text: I will even give them up to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth for evil, to be a reproach and a proverb, a taunt and a curse, in all places where I will drive them.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will even give them up to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth for evil, to be a reproach and a proverb.” Arminian readers see the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 coming to pass.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the covenant warnings fulfilled, citing Deuteronomy 28:37 by reference. Readers in this tradition read the verse soberly, as the outcome of persistent covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: I will send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence among them, until they are consumed from off the land that I gave to them and to their fathers.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence among them.” Arminian readers see the familiar triad of judgment in Jeremiah, repeated in the letter to the exiles in 29:17.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment completing the vision. Jeremiah 29:17 reuses the image of figs “so bad” they cannot be eaten, and readers in this tradition note the connection without harmonizing the two passages.
